reason: This passage (Exodus 14) explicitly frames the conflict as primarily religious and cosmic rather than political. The narrative centers on divine intervention and salvation: Moses instructs the Hebrews with 'יְשׁוּעַת יְהוָה' (the salvation of the LORD), declares 'יְהוָה יִלָּחֵם לָכֶם' (the LORD will fight for you), and attributes the deliverance to God's supernatural action—'כִּי יְהוָה נִלְחַם לָהֶם בְּמִצְרָיִם' (the LORD fought for them against Egypt). The Hebrews are portrayed as fearful, dependent, and doubtful—even expressing regret about leaving Egypt—relying entirely on God's intervention rather than exercising political agency or military power. The passage concludes with religious belief: 'וַיִּֽירְאוּ הָעָם אֶת־ יְהוָה וַיַּֽאֲמִ֙ינוּ֙ בַּֽיהוָה' (the people feared the LORD and believed in the LORD). While a political dimension exists (fleeing Egyptian authority, military pursuit), it is subordinate to the cosmic and religious framework that defines the narrative's meaning and resolution.
